analysis.one_liner: Imposes an annual tax on foreign owners of vacant U.S. homes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors in the last weeks of the 117th Congress, was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The American Property Act would put a 1% annual tax on foreign owners of U.S. homes that sit mostly empty. It covers single-family homes and buildings of up to four units (including condos and rowhouses), counting a home as "under-utilized" if it is occupied fewer than 180 days a year. The goal is to discourage foreign money from buying American housing and leaving it vacant while local residents face high prices and tight supply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary residents in communities where foreign-owned homes sit vacant. The tax gives foreign owners a reason to rent out or sell empty homes, which could add housing to the market and ease price pressure. Any revenue raised goes to the Treasury rather than to foreign holders of U.S. property.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents in markets with foreign-owned vacant homes

how_it_helps.text: It places a recurring cost on holding an American home empty: 1% of the property's value each year for any foreign owner whose property is occupied fewer than 180 days in the year [S2][S3].

The tax applies to the kinds of homes people actually live in — single-family homes, condos, rowhouses, and small buildings of four units or fewer — rather than large apartment towers, targeting the segment of housing where vacant investor-owned units compete directly with would-be homebuyers and renters [S3].
The tax base is the higher of the local property-tax appraisal or the most recent sale price, so the charge scales with the home's actual value rather than being a flat fee [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign persons (individuals or entities that are not U.S. persons) who own under-utilized U.S. residential property would pay 1% of the property's estimated value each year. Some of that cost could surface indirectly in sale prices if foreign owners offload homes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign owners of vacant U.S. homes

drawbacks.text: The occupancy test is strict for foreign owners: only U.S. citizens, permanent residents, or work-authorized people count as occupants, and stays must run at least a month to qualify, so a foreign owner's family visiting from abroad for weeks at a time would not shield the home from the tax [S3].

The tax is based on property value, not the owner's income, so it could fall on modest foreign-owned vacation homes as heavily as on investor-held mansions, and 1% of a home's value is a large recurring charge relative to typical rental income [S3].

Verifying how many days a home is actually occupied would be an administrative challenge for the IRS, and the bill leaves key terms like 'estimated value' appraisal methods to existing local practice, which varies widely [S3].
By targeting only foreign owners, the bill leaves vacancy by domestic owners and large corporate landlords untouched, limiting its effect on overall housing supply [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy aim — pushing empty foreign-owned homes into use — is popular and the tax is small enough that compliant owners could avoid it entirely by renting the home out, which is the point. But the bill is a narrow instrument: it only touches foreign-owned, mostly-vacant small residential properties, its occupancy rules are blunt, and enforcement would be difficult. It would likely produce modest housing and revenue gains rather than a broad fix, and its being offered with no cosponsors in the final days of a Congress suggests it was never built to clear the drafting and committee work a real tax change requires.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on December 15, 2022 — about two and a half weeks before the Congress ended — and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up before the session expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs (R-NY) introduced the bill on December 15, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation [S1][S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign owners of vacant or lightly used American homes keep their holdings free of any new annual tax, and nothing changed for communities where those homes sit empty.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign holders of vacant U.S. homes

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 15, 2022, in the final weeks of the 117th Congress

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to measure the split: the bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Foreign investors in U.S. residential real estate
industries.note: If enacted, the bill would charge these holders 1% of their property's value each year whenever a home sits occupied fewer than 180 days, creating a direct financial reason to rent or sell. Because the bill never advanced, their holdings remain untaxed.

industries.industry: U.S. residential real estate market (agents, brokers, and sellers to foreign buyers)
industries.note: A tax on foreign-owned vacant homes could reduce foreign demand for American housing and push some owners to sell, dampening the premium that offshore cash adds to home prices — good for local buyers, but a headwind for agents and sellers who profit from that demand.
